transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I can’t seem to stay focused long enough to get through all the reports and planning tasks my job requires anymore. I’ve always been able to manage my workload in the past, but lately, I feel completely overwhelmed trying to keep up.
Did these concentration problems start after a specific stressful life event or major change, or did they come on without any clear trigger? Around when did they begin?

I've actually had subtle focus and daydreaming issues since childhood, but they became severely problematic about two and a half years ago. It was triggered by a major promotion to manage a much larger service line, which dramatically increased my meetings and reports right as our health system went through a massive electronic record upgrade.

Before this promotion, did you have these attention problems in other parts of life too—like in school, at home, or in relationships—and did they cause trouble there? Or did they only become a problem after the work stress started?

They are definitely lifelong—even back in elementary school, teachers noted I daydreamed and missed instructions, and my parents had to sit with me for hours just to keep me on track with homework. Before my promotion, I managed to hide these struggles through extreme over-preparation, meticulous color-coded spreadsheets, and working late nights. However, the massive increase in my new work demands has finally overwhelmed my ability to compensate.

Besides work, are these attention problems currently causing noticeable difficulties in other parts of your life too, like managing household tasks, finances, appointments, or relationships? If so, which areas are most affected?

I haven't noticed major issues with my finances or relationships, mostly because I pour almost all of my extra energy and time into keeping up with work. However, I do find myself constantly misplacing things around the house, like my phone, glasses, or keys, which can be really frustrating.
When you were a child, did these attention problems show up in more than one setting—such as both at school and at home—and cause clear impairment in both? Can you give one example from each?

Yes, they definitely showed up in both places. At school, my teachers wrote on my report cards that I was smart but daydreamed and missed instructions, while at home, my parents had to sit with me at the kitchen table for hours because I'd constantly lose track of my homework.

Along with the inattention, have you also had lifelong problems with restlessness or impulsivity—like feeling driven to move, fidgeting, interrupting, or acting without thinking? If yes, which of those fit you best?

No, I don't really experience those symptoms of physical restlessness, fidgeting, or impulsivity. My struggles have always been much more focused on attention, drifting off, and maintaining mental focus rather than physical hyperactivity.

Besides daydreaming and losing focus, do you often make careless mistakes, have trouble finishing tasks, avoid work that needs sustained mental effort, or forget important things? Which of these happen most often for you right now?

I definitely struggle with both of those. I actively avoid mentally exhausting tasks like reading long regulatory updates by constantly finding excuses to get coffee or check my email. I also have a hard time finishing multi-step tasks, where I'll do the first part of an email request but completely forget the rest until someone chases me for it a week later.

Before these symptoms got much worse, were there any changes in sleep, anxiety/depression, alcohol or drug use, or medical issues like thyroid problems that could also affect concentration? If yes, which ones and when did they start?

No, I haven't had any major changes in my sleep, mood, or anxiety, and I don't use recreational drugs or have issues with alcohol. My primary care doctor actually did a full physical and checked my thyroid, and all my labs came back completely normal. She didn't find any medical issues, which is why she suggested my struggles might be undiagnosed ADHD.

opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Lifelong, cross-situational inattention beginning in childhood is clearly documented, with current clinically significant impairment at work and some home disorganization. Symptoms include daydreaming, missing instructions, difficulty sustaining attention, avoidance of sustained mental effort, failure to complete multi-step tasks, and frequent misplacing of items. Hyperactivity/impulsivity is denied, and alternative medical, substance-related, sleep, mood, and anxiety explanations were not supported.
